data.hypothesis: For large n, a separate output-zeroing launch followed by one grid-stride reduction launch should reduce launch and scratch-stage overhead versus the existing hierarchy. The tradeoff is one contended int32 atomic per CTA; using 256-thread CTAs, a target of 2048 elements per CTA, and a 1024-CTA cap tests whether this keeps input parallelism high enough without excessive aggregation contention. This remains an unmeasured hypothesis.
data.notes: The supplied baseline is valid and correct on 10 cases, with a reported mean of 46.67 microseconds over three samples. The provided T3 catalog has no prior candidate records or source-diversity observations, and there is no measured hierarchical candidate in the supplied context; therefore no comparison against one or candidate speed claim is possible here. The atomic path bypasses scratch; the original hierarchical path remains the fallback for smaller positive sizes. CUDA 12.6.3 Programming Guide and Best Practices Guide references were reported as consulted in the supplied Mother guidance: https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/archive/12.6.3/cuda-c-programming-guide/index.html and https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/archive/12.6.3/cuda-c-best-practices-guide/index.html. Controller correctness checks and repeated timings are still needed.
transformations: For n >= 1<<20, launch an ordered output-zeroing kernel before the reduction kernel on the default stream.
Use 256-thread CTAs to grid-stride over the input, combine each CTA's values with warp reductions, and perform exactly one int32 atomicAdd per CTA; choose ceil(n/2048) CTAs capped at 1024.
Retain the existing hierarchical reduction for smaller positive inputs and explicitly zero the output for n <= 0; the large-input atomic path does not use scratch.
